figures.caption: Table 1: Dimensions of evaluation for mesoscopic and whole-brain surrogate models. The table is deliberately score-free: each row states what an axis measures, why it does not collapse to a single number, and where the corresponding evidence or derivation is found in this review. It is meant to make explicit the space along which any principled benchmark must operate, and to expose how much of that space remains unmeasured for the lineage studied here, rather than to rank models.

Figure 1: Algorithmic work required to simulate one biological second for the model classes compared in this review, using the FLOP-equivalent convention detailed in Appendix C. Red curves correspond to mesoscopic and macroscopic mean-field models and are read against the bottom axis, which gives the number of brain regions K; blue dashed curves correspond to spiking neural networks and are read against the top axis, which gives the number of neurons N ; the gray dotted curve corresponds to TRIBE v2 and uses the same top scale as the number of predicted fMRI targets V . Among the meanfield curves, the two second-order variants differ in what covariances they track: the local version keeps finite-size covariances only within each node, preserving the same O(ρK2) whole-brain scaling as the first-order model, whereas the global version propagates covariances between all population variables of the network and therefore scales cubically (O(P 3K3)), which is why it separates from the other curves at large K. The plot uses P = 2 populations per node and a dense connectome (ρ = 1). Horizontal positions should therefore be compared only within the same colour family; the figure is intended to show scaling regimes and orders of magnitude, not a one-to-one equivalence between K, N , and V .

Figure 2: Algorithmic work per biological second for P = 10 populations per node. Increasing P mostly affects the node-local mean-field costs and strongly amplifies the global second-order covariance cost, whose leading term scales as O(P 3K3). Horizontal positions should be compared only within the same color family; the purpose of the figure is to show the scaling regimes and orders of magnitude rather than a one-to-one equivalence between K, N , and V .

Figure 3: Estimated memory traffic per biological second for P = 2 populations per node. Under the streaming-memory convention, dense mean-field models become dominated by connectome and delayed-state access, whereas spiking networks become dominated by sparse synaptic event traffic at sufficiently large N . TRIBE v2 is shown as a memory-footprint estimate rather than a stepwise integration traffic. Horizontal positions should be compared only within the same color family; the purpose of the figure is to show the scaling regimes and orders of magnitude rather than a one-to-one equivalence between K, N , and V .

Figure 4: Estimated memory traffic per biological second for P = 10 populations per node. The local state traffic increases with the number of populations, while the global second-order covariance model additionally carries a quadratic covariance footprint, scaling as O(P 2K2). Horizontal positions should be compared only within the same color family; the purpose of the figure is to show the scaling regimes and orders of magnitude rather than a one-to-one equivalence between K, N , and V .
